extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in philosophy (pragmatism, epistemology, religion)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains evaluative principles used in William James's lectures on pragmatism, especially standards for judging truth, hypotheses, and the human role in belief-formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'THE Truth' (plurality of truths)
rubrics_metrics.description: The question 'what is THE truth?' is no real question; THE Truth (one determinate, complete answer) is an abstraction from the plural facts of truth. Single-word or oracular answers (God, Reason, Law, etc.) are idols of the rationalistic mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat truth as a single pre-existent entity that simply awaits description; instead recognize multiple 'truths' that grow out of particular experiences. Example guidance: treat 'THE truth' like the phrase 'THE Latin Language' — a summarizing label rather than an antecedent reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truths are results / man-made products
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctions between true and false beliefs grow up incidentally among interactions of men's experiences; truth grafts itself on previous truth and modifies it in the process. Law, language, and truth are not antecedent principles but results produced over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging claims, treat them as creations built upon earlier beliefs and practices (e.g., judges 'twist' previous law into fresh law; idioms form from previous idiom plus innovation). Evaluate how a purported truth connects to and modifies previous truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatist criterion: meaning and truth judged by practical consequences/usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal conceptions and hypotheses have meaning only insofar as they have use; the meaning will be true if the use 'squares well with life's other uses.' If consequences useful to life flow from a hypothesis, it is real and meaningful for pragmatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess beliefs and hypotheses by asking what practical differences their acceptance makes. Use analogies (e.g., the word 'winter' as a useful summary of past experience) and test hypotheses by their bearings on life. The Absolute is legitimate for pragmatists if it produces useful religious or practical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for three parts of reality when forming beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reality, as something beliefs must take account of, consists of: (1) the flux of sensations (forced upon us and neither true nor false), (2) relations between sensations (two sub-parts: mutable/accidental relations like date/place, and fixed/essential inner relations like likeness), and (3) previous truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or formulating theories, explicitly consider how they handle each of these parts: do they respect immediate sensations, the inner relations perceptible on comparison, and the influence of prior accepted truths? Recognize that previous truths are less obdurate and often give way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective and emphasis shape which truths are formed
rubrics_metrics.description: Which aspects of sensation and relation we attend to, note, and emphasize depends on our interests; the same facts yield different formulations of truth depending on perspective (e.g., Waterloo is 'victory' for an Englishman and 'defeat' for a Frenchman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims with awareness of the agent's perspective and interests. Ask which elements were included or omitted and how emphasis produced the resultant truth-claim. This is a normative check against pretending neutrality when perspectives have shaped the account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and carving reality for human purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: We carve the flux of sensible reality into 'things' and assign predicates to suit human purposes (constellations, nouns, predicates). These are human additions that the sensible core passively tolerates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating classifications, names, or categories, justify them by the human purposes they serve; accept multiple equally 'true' ways of treating the same sensible datum and choose the one best suited to current purposes (e.g., whether to call a stellar group 'Charles's Wain' or 'Dipper').

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additions by whether they enhance the universe's total value
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions and human-made additions to reality should be judged by whether they 'enhance the universe's total value' — i.e., which human addition makes the best universe out of given material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use value-enhancement as a criterion: prefer formulations that yield worthier, more fruitful, or more coherent outcomes in life and thought. Example: Lotze and Eucken's suggestion that our descriptions may be important additions intended to 'raise' the given existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanism tempered by resisting factors of reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Although truths are man-made products (humanism), genuine pragmatists admit resisting factors in experience — sensations and relations — with which new truths must 'agree.' Beliefs contain human elements but must still 'know' the non-human element to count as knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pure caprice: creative or constructive accounts must take account of sensory input and inner relations. In practice, require that humanly-created beliefs accommodate the independent aspects of experience rather than contradict obvious facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: act as if the world is plastic until decisively rebuked
rubrics_metrics.description: Schiller's practical recommendation: we ought to 'start as if [the world] were wholly plastic, acting methodically on that assumption, and stopping only when we are decisively rebuked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a trial-and-error, experimental attitude toward hypotheses and practices: implement creative or reforming ideas and revise only in the face of decisive counter-evidence or rebuke. This prescribes a methodological boldness constrained by feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of hypotheses conditional on practical effects (abstract vs. concrete use of the Absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Absolute, or other metaphysical hypotheses, are legitimate for pragmatism if they have use: taken abstractly (like the word 'winter') they function as instrumental summaries of experience; taken concretely they may be religiously transformative and thus justified by their life-changing consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between instrumental/abstract uses of a conception (serviceable for orientation and planning) and concrete/religious uses (that change a person's life). Evaluate a metaphysical claim by assessing which use it serves and whether that use produces desirable, verifiable consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatism as mediator between tough-minded empiricism and tender-minded rationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Pragmatism mediates between empiricist 'tough-minded' insistence on facts and rationalist 'tender-minded' insistence on an eternal perfect edition; pragmatists accept hypotheses if they prove useful, avoiding both doctrinaire absolutism and unprincipled opportunism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adjudicating between opposing temperaments or systems, prefer hypotheses and practices that demonstrate practical payoff across life and thought. Guard against reducing pragmatism to mere opportunism by insisting on consequential tests rather than personal caprice.
